item.title: In 1988, ice covered 1.66 square miles near the summit of Indonesia's Puncak Jaya, and ...
item.summary: Ice appears light blue. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. In 1988, glaciers covered ...
item.page_text:
In 1988, glaciers covered about 1.66 square miles (4.31 square kilometers) near the summit of Puncak Jaya, on the island of New Guinea. By September 2025, about 0.03 square miles (0.09 square kilometers) were left.
That’s roughly 2 percent. What’s left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields.
It also no longer moves. The patches are too thin and too broken up to behave like a glacier, NASA Earth Observatory reported on November 16.
Puncak Jaya stands in the Sudirman Range, in the Indonesian part of New Guinea. Very few places this close to the equator have held ice all year round.
Next door is the largest stretch of warm ocean water on the planet. So the glaciers here sit near the warmest conditions in which year-round ice can survive at all.
Scientists have called them high-altitude canaries in the coal mine. Other members of that small club are what’s left of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania and the Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, a country that has lost more than half of its glaciers in six decades .
NASA compared two false-color pictures of the range. Landsat 5 took one on November 3, 1988. Landsat 9 took the other on October 19, 2026.
Ice shows up light blue, bare rock brown, clouds white and plants green. In 1988, blue caps several of the highest ridges. In 2026 there are only a few small blue fragments, and brown rock covers most of the old icy ridgetops.
The area figures come from Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at Indonesia’s Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics ( BMKG ). The 2025 number is based on satellite and aerial data.
An aerial survey is planned for December. It should show how much ice is left in 2026, Permana said.
The ice got thinner, too. At the main monitoring site, on the East Northwall Firn, it was 105 feet (32 meters) thick in 2010, Permana said.
In 2023 it measured 13 feet (4 meters). By November 2024 there was no ice there at all.
Thinning ice also cracks apart. Each new piece has fresh edges where it can melt, and so the losses feed on themselves.
In the 2026 image, newly bared rock sits between the remnants. Snow still falls on the mountain. It just doesn’t stay on the bare rock long enough to turn into new ice.
“It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has followed Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite images. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”
To count as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to do two things. It has to be thick enough to creep downhill under its own weight. And it needs a zone where snow piles up faster than it melts.
On Puncak Jaya, the ice is now so thin, and so split into small, stagnant patches, that it has stopped flowing.
“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said.
El Niño years are especially rough on these glaciers. Warmer air pushes the freezing level above the summit, so rain falls instead of snow.
Fresh snow is white. It bounces sunlight away and protects the ice underneath. Without it, the darker surface soaks up heat and melts faster.
During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than normal, a finding NASA links to a study in PNAS . In one year it lost roughly 17 feet (5.3 meters) of thickness.
Then came the 2023-2024 El Niño. The ice thinned again, by about 7 to 13 feet (2 to 4 meters) a year.
Recent satellite studies suggest the main ice areas could be gone completely around 2030. For this, NASA links a study published in The Cryosphere .
BMKG’s own estimates suggest the ice could disappear much sooner, Permana noted, with the current El Niño speeding things up. Either way, Puncak Jaya’s ice looks set to vanish well before Africa’s remaining glaciers, which may be gone by 2040 .
NASA links the 2 percent figure to a World Meteorological Organization report, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific 2025 .
The information was obtained from NASA Earth Observatory .

item.title: Satellite images suggest Russian corvette was hit in suspected drone attack in Benghazi
item.summary: Satellite images show Russian warship ablaze after suspected drone attack in Benghazi. Satellite imagery circulating on Sunday appeared to show a ...
item.page_text:
Satellite imagery circulating on Sunday appeared to show a Russian warship on fire at Benghazi’s naval base following overnight explosions, as Libya’s eastern-based government said preliminary investigations pointed to a suspected drone attack on a Russian vessel.
The images, reportedly captured by commercial satellite operator Planet at 7.47am local time on 22 November, showed flames and thick smoke rising from a vessel identified by military analysts as the Mercury, a Russian Steregushchiy-class corvette.
Naval analyst H I Sutton, who published the imagery, suggested the warship may have been completely destroyed. However, the extent of the damage and the vessel’s condition could not be independently established.
Ukrainian military intelligence-focused account ExileNova claimed the Russian Black Sea Fleet had lost the Mercury after a drone strike caused the vessel to sink in Benghazi harbour.
The account also alleged that the corvette had been involved in escorting Russian military cargo shipments to Libya and other African countries in support of Moscow’s Africa Corps operations. Those claims have not been independently confirmed.
Several other military monitoring accounts, including Visegrád 24, OSINTtechnical and NOELREPORTS, circulated reports of a possible drone attack near the northern berths of Benghazi port.
Separately, the military aviation monitoring account Faytuks Network reported that a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 aircraft associated with emergency services had flown towards Libya following the explosions. The purpose of the reported flight remains unclear.
Eastern government confirms investigation
The eastern-based government led by Prime Minister Osama Hammad said initial findings suggested that a Russian vessel docked at Benghazi naval base had been targeted by unmanned vehicles.
According to the government, the ship had stopped in Benghazi to replenish fuel and supplies while returning to Russia, under existing maritime cooperation arrangements.
The government said port facilities and the naval base had not sustained damage and announced a joint investigation with Russian authorities to establish the circumstances of the incident.
It described the suspected attack as a serious violation of Libyan sovereignty, stressing that Libya was not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine and should not become a venue for confrontation between foreign powers.
The statement followed an earlier account from emergency authorities in eastern Libya, which attributed the explosions to an ammunition storage incident at the naval base.
Tripoli warns against foreign military activity
Libya’s internationally recognised Government of National Unity, based in Tripoli, separately expressed serious concern over reports surrounding the Benghazi explosions.
In a statement, the government rejected the use of Libyan territory, ports and territorial waters for foreign military or logistical activities that could endanger national security.
It also warned against drawing Libya into conflicts between international powers, arguing that the incident highlighted the urgency of unifying the country’s military institutions under a single state authority.
The competing statements reflect the continuing division between Libya’s rival administrations, which exercise authority over different parts of the country.
The Mercury, commissioned into the Russian Navy in 2023, is a modern corvette approximately 105 metres long, with a crew of around 90 personnel.
The vessel previously attracted international attention in November 2024 amid reports of an incident involving a German naval helicopter in the Baltic Sea near the Danish island of Bornholm.
Germany raised concerns about reported warning fire involving a Russian vessel during the incident, which was subsequently discussed by then Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock at a NATO meeting in Brussels.
The latest developments in Benghazi have renewed attention on Russian naval operations in the Mediterranean and the use of Libyan ports by foreign military vessels.
Neither the identity of those responsible for the suspected attack nor the reported destruction of the Mercury has been independently established.
Russian authorities have not been quoted in the available accounts confirming the vessel’s loss or identifying those responsible for the incident.

item.title: Russian missile corvette “Merkuriy” went to the bottom, sank
item.summary: Satellite images show that the Russian missile corvette “Merkuriy”, attacked in the port of Benghazi, is almost completely underwater. Satellite ...
item.page_text:
Satellite images show that the Russian missile corvette “Merkuriy”, attacked in the port of Benghazi, is almost completely underwater.
Satellite images from the Vantor company taken after the attack on the “Merkuriy” were published online. They show that the ship has completely sunk.
Following the explosion on the Russian vessel in the port, ten people sustained minor injuries, medical sources told the agency. Among the injured are Russians and Libyans; they are receiving medical treatment in Benghazi.

item.title: Laser Focus at the Top of the World
item.summary: A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.
item.page_text:
A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.
More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a new, more precise method for tracking satellites.
Since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory —laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide.
In 2026, the next generation of SLR, developed by NASA scientists and tested at Goddard, began to come online. On October 12, a faster, even more precise SLR system officially debuted at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, operated by the Norwegian Mapping Authority, a NASA partner. The observatory’s remote location in the Arctic archipelago is shown in this image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 in July 2026. It is the first NASA next-generation SLR system in operation and the northernmost SLR facility on Earth.
While the systems developed decades ago have been “workhorses” of the global laser tracking network, their age and the growing number of satellites have necessitated updates, said Stephen Merkowitz, project manager for NASA’s Space Geodesy Project . “We wanted newer systems that could track more objects, and track them more accurately and precisely,” he said.
Years of development, testing, and careful calibration produced the Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system now running at Ny-Ålesund. Among its features are lasers that can fire pulses thousands of times per second, up from tens of times per second, and sensors that can detect single photons, meaning that less light needs to be reflected back from a satellite.
Along with determining the orbits of satellites, SLR is critical for establishing the terrestrial reference frame , the foundation of modern coordinate systems and a common standard that allows measurements to be compared with one another. “If you want to know where your satellite observation is on a map, you need to have it in the proper reference frame,” Merkowitz said. In addition, tracking Earth’s center of mass , measuring changes in sea level and ice mass, studying the motion of tectonic plates, and maintaining global navigation satellite systems such as GPS , all rely on an accurate reference frame.
The far-north location of the Ny-Ålesund facility improves the distribution of SLR stations across the planet, making the whole network more robust. The location also allows the system to gather more data about polar-orbiting satellites, which include ICESat-2 , GRACE-FO , and other Earth observation satellites. “From the station at Goddard [in Greenbelt, Maryland], we’ll catch the polar-orbiting satellites maybe two or three times a day,” Merkowitz said. “But from Ny-Ålesund, you’ll see them almost every orbit.”
Certain satellite missions may especially benefit from the Arctic location, he added. Take ICESat-2, designed to make precise observations of ice surface heights. Having a station tracking the satellite from an icy polar region could lead to more accurate measurements there. “When it’s over the ice, we want the calibration to be as good as possible,” Merkowitz said.
Innovations and lessons learned from the Svalbard installation will carry over to future ones, Merkowitz said. In particular, the Ny-Ålesund facility drove improvements in automation because the site is located next to a bird sanctuary . Access restrictions require the station to be remotely operated at certain times, such as during the summer breeding season for migratory birds. These capabilities can be refined and applied at other stations. NASA is currently building two more next-generation SLR systems to replace legacy instruments at Goddard and the McDonald Geodetic Observatory in Texas.
